questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.5
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What is the converse of the following assertion?

  • I stay only if you go
  1. I stay if you go
  2. If I stay then you go
  3. If you do not go then I do not stay
  4. If I do not stay then you go

review.independentCheck: Only if translates S implies G; the converse is G implies S.
review.notes: Only if translates S implies G; the converse is G implies S.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.6
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose $A$ is a finite set with $n$ elements. The number of elements in the largest equivalence relation of A is

  1. $n$
  2. $n^2$
  3. $1$
  4. $n+1$

review.independentCheck: The universal relation A cross A is the largest equivalence relation and has n squared pairs.
review.notes: The universal relation A cross A is the largest equivalence relation and has n squared pairs.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.7
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be two equivalence relations on a set. Consider the following assertions:

  1. $R_1 \cup R_2$ is an equivalence relation
  2. $R_1 \cap R_2$ is an equivalence relation

Which of the following is correct?

  1. Both assertions are true
  2. Assertions (i) is true but assertions (ii) is not true
  3. Assertions (ii) is true but assertions (i) is not true
  4. Neither (i) nor (ii) is true

review.independentCheck: Intersections preserve equivalence properties; two overlapping nonnested partitions make a nontransitive union.
review.notes: Intersections preserve equivalence properties; two overlapping nonnested partitions make a nontransitive union.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.8
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The number of functions from an $m$ element set to an $n$ element set is

  1. $m + n$
  2. $m^n$
  3. $n^m$
  4. $m*n$

review.independentCheck: Each of m inputs has n independent image choices, giving n^m functions.
review.notes: Each of m inputs has n independent image choices, giving n^m functions.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 1.23
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
How many sub strings of different lengths (non-zero) can be formed from a character string of length $n$?

  1. $n$
  2. $n^2$
  3. $2^n$
  4. $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$

review.independentCheck: Count start/end positions, n+(n-1)+...+1.
review.notes: Count start/end positions, n+(n-1)+...+1.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 2.1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The rank of the matrix given below is:

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 &4 &8 &7\\ 0 &0& 3 &0\\ 4 &2& 3 &1\\ 3 &12 &24 &21 \end{bmatrix}$$

  1. $3$
  2. $1$
  3. $2$
  4. $4$

review.independentCheck: The fourth row duplicates the first; the first three rows are independent, giving rank three.
review.notes: The fourth row duplicates the first; the first three rows are independent, giving rank three.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 2.2
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following determinant $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a & bc \\ 1 & b & ca \\ 1 & c & ab \end{vmatrix}$

Which of the following is a factor of $\Delta$?

  1. $a+b$
  2. $a-b$
  3. $a+b+c$
  4. $abc$

review.independentCheck: Row subtraction factors the determinant as (a-b)(a-c)(c-b).
review.notes: Row subtraction factors the determinant as (a-b)(a-c)(c-b).
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 2.3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The binary relation $R = \{(1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3), (3, 4)\}$ on the set $A=\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ is

  1. reflexive, symmetric and transitive

  2. neither reflexive, nor irreflexive but transitive

  3. irreflexive, symmetric and transitive

  4. irreflexive and antisymmetric

review.independentCheck: The missing (4,4) makes it neither reflexive nor irreflexive; checking its possible two-step paths confirms transitivity.
review.notes: The missing (4,4) makes it neither reflexive nor irreflexive; checking its possible two-step paths confirms transitivity.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 2.4
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
In a room containing $28$ people, there are $18$ people who speak English, $15$ people who speak Hindi and $22$ people who speak Kannada. $9$ persons speak both English and Hindi, $11$ persons speak both Hindi and Kannada whereas $13$ persons speak both Kannada and English. How many speak all three languages?

  1. $9$
  2. $8$
  3. $7$
  4. $6$

review.independentCheck: Three-set inclusion-exclusion gives 28=55-33+x, so x=6.
review.notes: Three-set inclusion-exclusion gives 28=55-33+x, so x=6.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1998 | Question: 3a
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml: Two friends agree to meet at a park with the following conditions. Each will reach the park between 4:00 pm and 5:00 pm and will see if the other has already arrived. If not, they will wait for 10 minutes or the end of the hour whichever is earlier and leave. What is the probability that the two will not meet?

review.independentCheck: The meeting band is the 60-by-60 square minus two 50-by-50 right triangles; nonmeeting probability is 25/36, within the stored NAT tolerance.
review.notes: The meeting band is the 60-by-60 square minus two 50-by-50 right triangles; nonmeeting probability is 25/36, within the stored NAT tolerance.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 1.1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The probability that it will rain today is $0.5$. The probability that it will rain tomorrow is $0.6$. The probability that it will rain either today or tomorrow is $0.7$. What is the probability that it will rain today and tomorrow?

  1. $0.3$
  2. $0.25$
  3. $0.35$
  4. $0.4$

review.independentCheck: Inclusion-exclusion gives intersection 0.5+0.6-0.7=0.4.
review.notes: Inclusion-exclusion gives intersection 0.5+0.6-0.7=0.4.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 1.3
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
The determinant of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -8 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

  1. $11$
  2. $-48$

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 3.1
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $\left(Z, *\right)$ be an algebraic structure where $Z$ is the set of integers and the operation $*$ is defined by $n*m = \max(n,m)$. Which of the following statements is true for $\left(Z, *\right)$?

  1. $\left(Z, *\right)$ is a monoid
  2. $\left(Z, *\right)$ is an Abelian group
  3. $\left(Z, *\right)$ is a group
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: max has no identity on all integers because the integers have no least element.
review.notes: max has no identity on all integers because the integers have no least element.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 3.2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following propositions is a tautology?

  1. $(p \vee q) \rightarrow p$
  2. $p \vee (q \rightarrow p)$
  3. $p \vee (p \rightarrow q)$
  4. $p \rightarrow (p \rightarrow q)$

review.independentCheck: Option C simplifies to a propositional tautology; simple truth assignments refute A, B, and D.
review.notes: Option C simplifies to a propositional tautology; simple truth assignments refute A, B, and D.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 4.2
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n$-rowed square matrix and $I_{12}$ be the matrix obtained by interchanging the first and second rows of the $n$-rowed Identity matrix. Then $AI_{12}$ is such that its first

  1. Row is the same as its second row
  2. Row is the same as the second row of $A$
  3. Column is the same as the second column of $A$
  4. Row is all zero

questions.title: GATE CSE 1997 | Question: 6.1
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
A partial order $≤$ is defined on the set $S=\left \{ x, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, y \right \}$ as $x$ $\leq _{i}$ $a_{i}$ for all $i$ and $a_{i}\leq y$ for all $i$, where $n ≥ 1$. The number of total orders on the set S which contain the partial order $≤$ is

  1. $n!$
  2. $n+2$
  3. $n$
  4. $1$

review.independentCheck: x must be first, y last, and the n middle elements are freely permutable.
review.notes: x must be first, y last, and the n middle elements are freely permutable.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1996 | Question: 1.1
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets and let $A^c$ and $B^c$ denote the complements of the sets $A$ and $B$. The set $(A-B) \cup (B-A) \cup (A \cap B)$ is equal to

  1. $A \cup B$

  2. $A^c \cup B^c$

  3. $A \cap B$

  4. $A^c \cap B^c$

questions.title: GATE CSE 1996 | Question: 1.2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $X = \{2, 3, 6, 12, 24\}$, Let $\leq$ be the partial order defined by $X \leq Y$ if $x$ divides $y$. Number of edges in the Hasse diagram of $(X, \leq)$ is

  1. $3$
  2. $4$
  3. $9$
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: The divisibility cover relations are 2-6, 3-6, 6-12, 12-24.
review.notes: The divisibility cover relations are 2-6, 3-6, 6-12, 12-24.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1996 | Question: 1.3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are sets and $|X| \text{ and } |Y|$ are their respective cardinality. It is given that there are exactly $97$ functions from $X$ to $Y$. From this one can conclude that

  1. $|X| =1, |Y| =97$
  2. $|X| =97, |Y| =1$
  3. $|X| =97, |Y| =97$
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: 97 is prime, so n^m=97 forces m=1,n=97.
review.notes: 97 is prime, so n^m=97 forces m=1,n=97.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

  2. The set of integers in an abelian group under addition
  3. The set of rational numbers form an abelian group under multiplication
  4. The set of real numbers excluding zero is an abelian group under multiplication

review.independentCheck: Zero has no multiplicative inverse in Q.
review.notes: Zero has no multiplicative inverse in Q.
